AI Summary

The clearest can't-miss item this cycle is Cedric Feschotte's review Feschotte in Nature Reviews Genetics, arguing that TE-derived sequences are a recurring, general-purpose substrate for regulatory and coding innovation across the tree of life — effectively an updated companion to the lab's own 2017 NRG review, with a decade of new exaptation examples. Paired with it, Schnabl-Baumgartner et al. in Molecular Cell resolve a genuine mechanistic gap in SINE regulation: the ChAHP complex (CHD4-ADNP-HP1) silences SINE B2 elements not by heterochromatin formation but by directly blocking TFIIIB recruitment to the Pol III promoter — a fundamentally different silencing logic than the H3K9me3/KRAB-ZFP paradigm we normally invoke for ERVs like MER41 and LTR10. Rounding out the top tier, the TIPs framework in Genome Biology is worth close reading for anyone touching LTR10/LTR18: a deep-learning proteogenomic pipeline that finds 20-fold more TE-derived HLA-presented peptides than conventional immunopeptidomics, including tumor-specific antigens induced by epigenetic therapy — the antigen-presentation counterpart to the TE-reactivation-in-cancer story the lab has been building from the enhancer side.

Several papers extend the mechanistic vocabulary for how TEs get regulated and repurposed. Zhu et al. map CTCF binding site (CBS) evolution across five primates and find distinct TE families differentially contribute to conserved versus human-specific CBSs — directly analogous to the MER41/AIM2 story, but for 3D genome architecture rather than IFN-inducible enhancers, and worth citing wherever we discuss TE-driven regulatory rewiring in primates. In a conceptually adjacent paper, Weaver & Lowe show segmental duplication is a second, non-TE mechanism for building co-regulatory element families with shared motifs — a useful foil when arguing TEs are special (a single TE family can seed thousands of dispersed copies genome-wide in one event; segmental duplication cannot). On the plant side, a DNA break-5mC cycle reactivates TEs in Arabidopsis following unrepaired ssDNA lesions — a mechanistically clean example of genotoxic stress unlocking TE expression that pairs well with our cancer-genotoxic-stress framing for TE reactivation.

On the immune/cancer side, the most mechanistically important paper is Guo et al. in Immunity: lactate produced by PKM2-phosphorylated LDHA (Ser161) binds the cGAMP-binding domain of STING directly, blocking IRF3 activation and immune infiltration in glioblastoma, and PKM2 inhibition restores STING signaling and synergizes with anti-PD-1. This bears directly on the viral-mimicry/EHMT-G9A axis — STING is the shared downstream node that G9A/EHMT2 inhibition activates via dsRNA sensing, so a tumor-intrinsic metabolic brake on STING is a competing suppressive mechanism worth citing in that aim. The DOT1L-MED23 glioblastoma enhancer paper and the multi-STING-agonist mRNA-LNP vaccine platform bracket this nicely — one on the epigenetic-enhancer side of GBM growth, one on the therapeutic side of reactivating STING in tumors.

Finally, two sequence-to-function papers are must-reads for the AlphaGenome-adjacent modeling direction: Aksu & Vingron's Corgi integrates DNA sequence with trans-regulator expression to extrapolate chromatin accessibility and expression into held-out cell types (a real gap in current S2F models), while Spiro et al.'s SAGE-net trains S2F models directly on personal genomes and finds gains come mostly from flagging individual variants rather than learning a generalizable cis-regulatory grammar — a sobering result directly relevant to how we frame polymorphic TE insertions in the pan-genome work. On the isoform side, EZbakR extends isoform-resolved kinetic modeling to nonsense-mediated decay, exposing large NMD-efficiency differences between transcripts of the same gene — a useful analytical framework for the IL18R1/IL2RB isoform work, where TE-derived exons are likely to show exactly this kind of isoform-specific decay heterogeneity.
